title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt V: At Heorot’s Door (lines 320–370)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 13–14, lines 320–370 (fitt V). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Strǣt wæs stānfāh, stīg wīsode
gumum ætgædere.
sentences.l: The street was stone-variegated; the path showed-the-way to the men together.
sentences.i: The road was paved with stones of many colours, and the path led the men on together.
sentences.n: ‘Strǣt’ is the Latin ‘strata’ (‘paved way’) taken into Old English, the word also in ‘lagustrǣte’ (‘sea-street’) in Fitt III. ‘Wæs’ links it to ‘stānfāh’, a predicate adjective meaning ‘stone-variegated’; ‘fāh’ means ‘coloured, patterned, gleaming’ (compare ‘fāh ond fȳrheard’ of the helmets in Fitt IV), so the road is pictured as laid with stones of different colours. That picture is a guess: the compound occurs only here, and it could mean no more than ‘stony’. In the second clause ‘stīg’ (‘path’) is the singular subject of ‘wīsode’, ‘showed the way’ (the verb of ‘wīsade’ and ‘wīsige’ in Fitts III and IV), and ‘gumum’ is a dative plural, ‘to the men’. ‘ætgædere’ is ‘together’. After the sea-landing and the guard's leave-taking in Fitt IV, the Geats now march up the Danish road to the hall, which this passage does not yet name.

sentences.t:
Gūðbyrne scān
heard hondlocen, hringīren scīr
song in searwum, þā hīe tō sele furðum
in hyra gryregeatwum gangan cwōmon.
sentences.l: The war-byrnie shone, hard, hand-locked; the bright ring-iron sang in the armor, when they to the hall, just then, in their terror-gear came to go.
sentences.i: Their war-mail shone, hard and linked by hand, and the bright iron rings sang in the armor as they came walking, just then, toward the hall in their fearsome gear.
sentences.n: Two main clauses come first, each with its own subject, and then a clause of time. ‘Gūðbyrne’ (‘war-byrnie’, a shirt of mail) is the subject of ‘scān’, ‘shone’ (past of ‘scīnan’, as in ‘scionon’ in Fitt IV), and ‘heard hondlocen’ (‘hard, hand-locked’) describes it: the rings are linked together by hand. ‘hringīren’ (‘ring-iron’, mail) is the subject of ‘song’, ‘sang’, with ‘scīr’ (‘bright’) beside it; mail ‘sings’ when it moves. ‘þā hīe … gangan cwōmon’ is ‘when they came to go’, an infinitive after ‘cwōmon’, in the construction ‘came walking’. ‘furðum’ is a dative-plural form used as an adverb, ‘just, just then, at first’; the apparatus records ‘furður’, ‘farther’, from Trautmann (its ‘Tr.’; his Bonner Beiträge appear as ‘Tr. Bonn. B.’ elsewhere in the apparatus), which would give ‘came farther toward the hall’, and Klaeber prints ‘furðum’. ‘gryregeatwum’ is a dative plural, ‘in their terror-gear’ (‘gryre’, ‘terror’; ‘geatwe’, ‘equipment’), meaning armor that frightens.

sentences.t:
Setton sǣmēþe sīde scyldas,
rondas regnhearde wið þæs recedes weal;
sentences.l: Sea-weary they set their wide shields, shield-rims mightily hard, against the hall's wall;
sentences.i: Weary from the sea, they set their broad shields, the shield-rims exceedingly hard, against the wall of the hall;
sentences.n: ‘Setton’ is the past plural of ‘settan’, ‘set’, with no subject stated; it is the Geats of the previous unit. ‘sǣmēþe’ is a nominative plural, ‘sea-weary’ (‘sǣ’, ‘sea’; ‘mēþe’, ‘tired’). ‘sīde scyldas’ and ‘rondas regnhearde’ are two object phrases for the same shields: ‘rond’ is the rim (and so the shield), the same word as ‘rand’ in ‘randas’ in Fitt III, and ‘sīde’ is ‘wide’. ‘regnhearde’ has an intensifying first part, ‘regn-’, which the lexica gloss ‘mighty’; ‘mightily hard’ is a guess at the force of a compound found only here. ‘wið þæs recedes weal’ is ‘against the hall's wall’: ‘wið’ takes the accusative ‘weal’, and ‘reced’ (‘hall’, as in ‘receda’ in Fitt IV) is in the genitive.

sentences.t:
bugon þā tō bence, — byrnan hringdon,
gūðsearo gumena;
sentences.l: bowed then to the bench, — byrnies rang, the men's war-gear;
sentences.i: then they sat down on the bench, and their mail-shirts rang, the men's war-gear;
sentences.n: ‘bugon’ is the past plural of ‘būgan’, ‘bend, bow’; with ‘tō bence’ (‘to the bench’, a dative of ‘benc’) it means ‘they sat down’. The dash is Klaeber's: it joins a second clause to the first, saying what else happened as they sat. ‘byrnan hringdon’ is ‘byrnies rang’, with ‘hringdon’ the past plural of ‘hringan’, ‘to ring’, the plural verb for the plural subject ‘byrnan’. ‘gūðsearo gumena’ is ‘war-gear of men’, with ‘gumena’ a genitive plural; the phrase repeats ‘byrnan’ in other words, and this habit of saying a thing twice is common in the poem. The mail that sang as they walked (323) now rings as they lower themselves onto the benches.

sentences.l: spears stood, the seamen's gear all together, ash-wood gray above;
sentences.i: their spears stood together, the seamen's weapons, the ash shafts grey at the top;
sentences.n: ‘gāras stōdon’ is ‘spears stood’, nominative plural with a past plural verb. ‘sǣmanna searo’ is ‘the sea-men's gear’: ‘sǣmanna’ is a genitive plural, and ‘searo’ is a nominative in apposition to ‘gāras’, explaining it, and ‘samod ætgædere’ is two words for ‘together’ in a row. ‘æscholt’ is ‘ash-wood’ (‘æsc’, the ash tree and also a spear made of it; ‘holt’, ‘wood’), a collective singular for the shafts. ‘ufan grǣg’ is ‘gray above’; the picture of iron spearheads on top of the shafts is a guess, because the phrase does not say what is gray. ‘grǣg’ is the word that appears in the plural ‘grǣge syrcan’ (‘gray mail-shirts’) at 334.

sentences.t:
wæs se īrenþrēat
wǣpnum gewurþad.
sentences.l: was the iron-troop with weapons honored.
sentences.i: and the band of iron-clad men was graced by its weapons.
sentences.n: ‘wæs … gewurþad’ is a passive, ‘was honored, adorned’; ‘gewurþad’ is the participle of ‘geweorðian’ (as in ‘wǣpnum geweorðad’ in Fitt III), and ‘wǣpnum’ is a dative of means, ‘with weapons’. ‘īrenþrēat’ is ‘iron-troop’: ‘īren’ is iron, and ‘þrēat’ is a band, a throng (the word is the ancestor of ‘threat’ in the sense of ‘crowd’). Mail and weapons make the company look like a body of iron. The clause begins in mid-line, after the semicolon, because Klaeber punctuates across the line.

sentences.t:
Þā ðǣr wlonc hæleð
ōretmecgas æfter æþelum frægn:
sentences.l: Then there a proud hero asked the warriors about their noble-descents:
sentences.i: Then a proud man there questioned the warriors about their lineage:
sentences.n: ‘frægn’ is the past of ‘frignan’, ‘ask’ (compare ‘gefrægn’ and ‘frægn’ in Fitt III), and takes the person asked in the accusative, ‘ōretmecgas’, and the thing asked about after ‘æfter’ with the dative, ‘æþelum’. ‘wlonc hæleð’ is ‘proud hero’; ‘wlonc’ means ‘proud, splendid’, and ‘hæleð’ is ‘man, hero’. The poem does not name him here. At 348 Wulfgār answers the Geat leader's reply, which makes him the questioner, and he is the ‘ār ond ombiht’, ‘messenger and officer’, who describes himself at 335. ‘ōretmecgas’ is ‘battle-men’ (‘ōret’, ‘fight’; ‘mecg’, ‘man’), a poetic word for warriors. ‘æþelum’ is an emendation. Klaeber prints the letters ‘æþel’ in italic, his mark for letters he has changed, and the apparatus reports that the manuscript has ‘hæleþum’, which would read ‘asked the warriors after the heroes’ and repeats ‘hæleð’ from this very line. Grein proposed ‘æþelum’ (‘æþelu’, ‘noble descent’), and the apparatus cites line 392 as his parallel, where ‘ēower æþelu can’ means ‘knows your noble descent’, with the same noun; so the sense is ‘asked about their ancestry’. The colon opens the speech.

sentences.t:
‘Hwanon ferigeað gē fǣtte scyldas,
grǣge syrcan, ond grīmhelmas,
heresceafta hēap?
sentences.l: ‘Whence do you bear plated shields, gray mail-shirts, and mask-helmets, a heap of army-shafts?
sentences.i: ‘From where do you bring these plated shields, grey mail-shirts and helmets with face-masks, this heap of spears?
sentences.n: ‘Hwanon’ is ‘from where’, and ‘ferigeað gē’ is ‘do you carry’: the verb stands before its subject, as in a question, in the present plural of ‘ferian’. The three objects are accusative plurals: ‘fǣtte scyldas’, ‘grǣge syrcan’ and ‘grīmhelmas’, with ‘heresceafta hēap’ added at the end. ‘fǣtte’ is probably ‘plated, ornamented’, from a word for a plate of metal (a guess; the form is not common). ‘grīmhelmas’ is ‘mask-helmets’: ‘grīma’ is a mask, and the helmet has a face-guard. ‘heresceafta’ is a genitive plural, ‘of army-shafts’, meaning spears; ‘hēap’ is a ‘heap’ or throng, so ‘a heap of spears’ is a blunt phrase for the whole armed company. The question mark ends the first question; the speaker then introduces himself.

sentences.t:
Ic eom Hrōðgāres
ār ond ombiht. Ne seah ic elþēodịge
þus manige men mōdiglīcran.
sentences.l: I am Hrothgar's messenger and officer. Not saw I foreign men, so many, more proud-looking.
sentences.i: I am Hrothgar's herald and officer. I have never seen so many foreign men who looked prouder.
sentences.n: ‘Ic eom … ār ond ombiht’ is ‘I am messenger and officer’: two nouns that name one office, with ‘Hrōðgāres’ a genitive, ‘Hrothgar's’. ‘ār’ here is the masculine noun ‘messenger’, a different word from the feminine ‘ār’, ‘honor’, in ‘ārstafum’ (Fitt IV). ‘ombiht’ is ‘servant, officer’ and the same word as ‘ombeht’ in Fitt IV, spelled differently. ‘Ne seah ic’ is ‘I did not see’, with ‘seah’ the past of ‘sēon’. ‘elþēodịge’ (‘foreign’, from ‘el-’, ‘other’, and ‘þēod’, ‘people’) agrees with ‘men’; the dot under the ‘i’ is Klaeber's sign that this vowel does not count in the metre, so the word is scanned as if the vowel were not there. ‘þus manige’ is ‘thus many’ and ‘mōdiglīcran’ the comparative ‘more proud-looking’, ‘mōdig’ meaning ‘high-spirited, proud, bold’.

sentences.t:
Wēn’ ic þæt gē for wlenco, nalles for wræcsīðum,
ac for higeþrymmum Hrōðgār sōhton.’
sentences.l: I expect that you out of pride, not at all out of exile-journeys, but out of mind-might, sought Hrothgar.’
sentences.i: I think you have sought Hrothgar out of pride and strength of mind, and not as men driven into exile.’
sentences.n: The apostrophe after ‘Wēn’ is Klaeber's mark of elision: the full form is ‘wēne ic’, ‘I expect’ (the first person of ‘wēnan’, as in ‘þæs ic wēne’ at 271), and the final ‘e’ is lost before ‘ic’. The clause after ‘þæt’ has ‘gē’ as its subject and ‘Hrōðgār’ as the object of ‘sōhton’, ‘sought’, which stands at the end of the unit. ‘for wlenco’ is ‘for pride’ (the noun ‘wlenco’ goes with ‘wlonc’, ‘proud’), and ‘for higeþrymmum’ is ‘for mind-might’, from ‘hige’, ‘mind’, and ‘þrymm’, ‘might, glory’; ‘for’ with the dative gives the reason, ‘out of’. ‘nalles’ is ‘not at all’ and ‘wræcsīðum’ is ‘exile-journeys’ (‘wræc’, ‘banishment’; ‘sīð’, ‘journey’), so ‘nalles … ac’ is ‘not … but’. The apparatus entry ‘Fol. 137b þrymmum’ marks where manuscript leaf 137 verso begins. The closing quotation mark ends the questioner's speech, and the Geat leader answers in the next unit.

sentences.t:
Him þā ellenrōf andswarode,
wlanc Wedera lēod, word æfter spræc
heard under helme:
sentences.l: To him then the valor-bold one answered, the proud man of the Weders, a word afterwards spoke, hard under helmet:
sentences.i: Then the man bold in valor answered him, the proud man of the Weders, and spoke his answer, stern under his helmet:
sentences.n: ‘Him’ is a dative because ‘andswarode’ takes the dative of the one answered, as in Fitt IV. The poem has not yet named the speaker: ‘ellenrōf’ (‘ellen’, ‘valor’; ‘rōf’, ‘bold’, as in ‘higerōf’ in Fitt III) and ‘wlanc Wedera lēod’ are two epithets for the Geat leader; ‘wlanc’ is a variant spelling of ‘wlonc’ at 331. ‘lēod’ in the singular is ‘man, prince’; ‘Wedera’ is a genitive plural, ‘of the Weders’, another name for the Geats. ‘word æfter spræc’ is ‘spoke a word afterwards’, the same formula as ‘word æfter cwæð’ in Fitt IV, and means ‘spoke in turn’. ‘heard under helme’ is ‘hard under helmet’: ‘heard’ can mean ‘stern, brave’, and ‘helme’ is a dative after ‘under’ with the helmet still on. The colon opens his speech.

sentences.t:
‘Wē synt Higelāces
bēodgenēatas;
sentences.l: ‘We are Higelac's table-companions;
sentences.i: ‘We are companions at Higelac's table;
sentences.n: ‘Wē synt’ is ‘we are’, and ‘bēodgenēatas’ is the predicate, a nominative plural. ‘bēod’ here is ‘table’ (the word also meant a bowl), and ‘genēat’ is one who shares something, so ‘table-companions’ names retainers who eat at their lord's board; Fitt IV has the matching word ‘heorðgenēatas’, ‘hearth-companions’. ‘Higelāces’ is a genitive. As in Fitt IV, he names his lord before himself.

sentences.t: Bēowulf is mīn nama.
sentences.l: Beowulf is my name.
sentences.i: Beowulf is my name.
sentences.n: ‘Bēowulf is mīn nama’ is a short equation: ‘is’ links the subject ‘Bēowulf’ and ‘nama’, ‘name’, with ‘mīn’, ‘my’. Here the poem first names the Geat hero; Fitt III called him only ‘Higelāces þegn’. A Bēowulf of the Danes appears in the prologue, a different man with the same name.

sentences.t:
Wille ic āsecgan sunu Healfdenes,
mǣrum þēodne mīn ǣrende,
aldre þīnum, gif hē ūs geunnan wile,
þæt wē hine swā gōdne grētan mōton.’
sentences.l: I will announce to the son of Healfdene, to the famed lord, my errand, to your chief, if he will grant us, that we him, so good a one, greet may.’
sentences.i: I will tell the son of Healfdene, that famed lord, my errand — your lord, I mean — if he will grant that we may greet him, good as he is.’
sentences.n: ‘Wille ic āsecgan’ is ‘I will announce’ with a dative of the person told and an accusative of the thing: ‘mǣrum þēodne’ and ‘aldre þīnum’ are datives (‘to the famed lord’, ‘to your chief’), and ‘mīn ǣrende’ is the thing told, ‘my errand’. ‘sunu Healfdenes’ stands beside them and should be a dative, ‘suna’; the apparatus shows that Kemble, others and Sedgefield print ‘suna’, while Klaeber prints ‘sunu’ and the apparatus sends the reader to ‘Lang. § 18.2’, a numbered section that this transcription does not include, so his reason is not known here. The sense is the same. ‘aldor’ is ‘lord, chief’ here (it also means ‘life’); ‘þīnum’ (‘your’) shows that Wulfgār's lord is meant. ‘gif hē ūs geunnan wile’ is ‘if he will grant us’, ‘geunnan’ (‘to grant’) taking the dative. ‘þæt wē hine … grētan mōton’ is ‘that we may greet him’, with ‘mōton’ the present plural of ‘mōtan’, ‘may, be allowed’ (the clause states the favor asked), and ‘swā gōdne’ is ‘so good’, ‘good as he is’. The closing mark ends Beowulf's speech.

sentences.t:
Wulfgār maþelode — þæt wæs Wendla lēod,
wæs his mōdsefa manegum gecȳðed,
wīg ond wīsdōm —:
sentences.l: Wulfgar spoke in speech-words — that was the Wendels' man, his mind-spirit was to many made known, war and wisdom —:
sentences.i: Wulfgar spoke in formal words — he was a man of the Wendels, and his spirit was known to many, in war and in wisdom —:
sentences.n: ‘Wulfgār maþelode’ follows the formula already used: ‘maþelode’ is ‘spoke in speech-words’ (‘spoke in formal words’), as at 286 in Fitt IV. The two dashes enclose a parenthesis about the speaker, and the colon after the second one opens his speech. Inside it, ‘þæt wæs Wendla lēod’ is ‘that was a man of the Wendels’ (‘Wendla’ a genitive plural; ‘lēod’ ‘man, prince’), and ‘wæs his mōdsefa manegum gecȳðed’ is a passive, ‘his spirit was made known to many’, with ‘manegum’ a dative plural and ‘mōdsefa’ a compound of ‘mōd’ (‘spirit, mind’) and ‘sefa’ (‘mind’) meaning ‘heart, character’. ‘wīg ond wīsdōm’ (‘war and wisdom’) adds what was known: his fighting and his good sense. The Wendels (‘Wendlas’) are named only here in the poem, and where they lived is a guess; the Vandals and the people of Vendel in Sweden have been suggested, and neither is certain. He is the man who questioned the Geats at 331: he answers the Geat leader's reply, and he is the ‘ār ond ombiht’ of 335.

sentences.t:
‘Ic þæs wine Deniga,
frēan Scildinga frīnan wille,
bēaga bryttan, swā þū bēna eart,
þēoden mǣrne ymb þīnne sīð,
ond þē þā andsware ǣdre gecȳðan,
ðē mē se gōda āgifan þenceð.’
sentences.l: ‘I of this will ask the friend of the Danes, the lord of the Scyldings, the rings' dispenser, as you a petitioner are, the famed lord, about your journey, and to you the answer quickly make known, which to me the good one intends to give.’
sentences.i: ‘I will ask the friend of the Danes, the lord of the Scyldings, the giver of rings, that famed lord, about your journey, as you request, and will soon make known to you the answer that the good king means to give me.’
sentences.n: ‘Ic … frīnan wille’ is ‘I will ask’; ‘frīnan’ takes the genitive of the matter, ‘þæs’ (‘about this’), and the accusative of the person asked, which is stretched over four phrases: ‘wine Deniga’ (‘friend of the Danes’: ‘wine’, ‘friend’, is an accusative singular and ‘Deniga’ a genitive plural), ‘frēan Scildinga’ (‘lord of the Scyldings’, as in Fitt IV with another spelling), ‘bēaga bryttan’ (‘giver of rings’, as in the prologue, the generous lord) and ‘þēoden mǣrne’ (‘famed lord’), all naming Hrothgar. ‘ymb þīnne sīð’ is ‘about your journey’. ‘swā þū bēna eart’ is ‘as you are a petitioner’, so ‘as you ask’. ‘ond þē … gecȳðan’ is a second infinitive after ‘wille’, ‘and make known to you’; ‘ǣdre’ is ‘soon, at once’. ‘þā andsware’ is the object, and ‘ðē’ is the relative particle, ‘which’, and its clause is ‘mē se gōda āgifan þenceð’: ‘the good one’ (Hrothgar) intends ‘to give’ (‘āgifan’) it ‘to me’ (‘mē’). ‘þenceð’ is ‘intends’. The mark at the end closes the speech.

sentences.t:
Hwearf þā hrædlīce þǣr Hrōðgār sæt
eald ond anhār mid his eorla gedriht;
sentences.l: Turned then quickly to where Hrothgar sat, old and wholly gray, with his earls' company;
sentences.i: Then he went quickly to where Hrothgar sat, old and white-haired, among the company of his earls;
sentences.n: ‘Hwearf’ is the past of ‘hweorfan’, ‘turn, go’ (compare ‘hwurfe’ in Fitt IV), with the subject Wulfgār unstated; ‘þǣr Hrōðgār sæt’ is ‘where Hrothgar sat’, and ‘eald ond anhār’ describe Hrothgar. ‘anhār’ is an emendation: Klaeber prints the first letter ‘a’ in italic, and the apparatus reports that the manuscript has ‘un hár’, two words. ‘un-’ as the negative prefix would give ‘not gray’, which cannot go with ‘eald’, so the usual remedy, which the apparatus credits to Trautmann (its ‘Tr.’, once with a page reference and a query), Holthausen and Chambers, reads ‘an-’; ‘wholly gray’ is a guess at what ‘an-’ adds. ‘mid his eorla gedriht’ is ‘with his company of earls’: ‘gedriht’ (‘company, troop’) is the object of ‘mid’, and ‘eorla’ a genitive plural.

sentences.t:
ēode ellenrōf, þæt hē for eaxlum gestōd
Deniga freân; cūþe hē duguðe þēaw.
sentences.l: went the valor-bold one, until he before the shoulders stood of the Danes' lord; he knew the retinue's custom.
sentences.i: He went, bold in valor, until he stood close before the lord of the Danes; he knew the custom of the court.
sentences.n: ‘ēode’ is the past of ‘gān’, ‘go’. ‘ellenrōf’ is the epithet of Beowulf at 340, here given to Wulfgār, so the poem does not keep it for the hero. ‘þæt hē … gestōd’ is ‘until he stood’ with ‘þæt’ here meaning ‘until’. ‘for eaxlum’ is ‘before the shoulders’, a phrase for standing directly in front of someone; ‘eaxl’ is the shoulder, and the dative plural follows ‘for’. ‘Deniga freân’ is ‘of the lord of the Danes’: ‘freân’ belongs to a weak noun whose ending -an serves for the genitive, dative and accusative, and here it is a genitive depending on ‘eaxlum’, with ‘Deniga’ a genitive plural; the circumflex is Klaeber's mark for a contracted vowel (‘freân’ in Fitt IV). After the semicolon, ‘cūþe hē duguðe þēaw’ is ‘he knew the custom of the retinue’: ‘cūþe’ is the past of ‘cunnan’, ‘know’; ‘duguðe’ is a genitive of ‘duguð’, the seasoned body of warriors around a king; ‘þēaw’ is ‘custom’, English ‘thew’ is its descendant. He knows how to approach a king.

sentences.t: Wulfgār maðelode tō his winedrihtne:
sentences.l: Wulfgar spoke in speech-words to his friend-lord:
sentences.i: Wulfgar spoke in formal words to his lord and friend:
sentences.n: ‘maðelode’ is the same verb as ‘maþelode’ at 348, with ‘ð’ for ‘þ’, and the house rendering is the same: ‘spoke in speech-words’, ‘spoke in formal words’. ‘tō his winedrihtne’ is a dative, ‘to his friend-lord’: ‘wine’ is ‘friend’ and ‘drihten’ ‘lord, leader of a war-band’; the word names a lord who is also a friend. The apparatus records that a new manuscript leaf (folio 138 recto) begins at ‘tō’. The colon opens the speech.

sentences.t:
‘Hēr syndon geferede, feorran cumene
ofer geofenes begang Gēata lēode;
sentences.l: ‘Here are journeyed, from afar come, over the ocean's circuit, Geat-people;
sentences.i: ‘Here are men of the Geat people, travelled from afar, come across the wide ocean;
sentences.n: ‘Hēr syndon’ is ‘here are’, and the subject, ‘Gēata lēode’ (‘people of the Geats’, a nominative plural), is held to the end of 362. ‘geferede’ is a participle; it is taken as ‘journeyed’, from ‘gefēran’, ‘to travel’, a guess, since a similar form from ‘geferian’ would mean ‘brought’. ‘feorran cumene’ is ‘come from far’, a participle of ‘cuman’; Klaeber prints it as two words, and the apparatus lists two scholars (‘Klu.’ and ‘Holt.’) who print it as one. ‘ofer geofenes begang’ is ‘over the ocean's circuit’: ‘geofon’ is ‘ocean’ (here a genitive), and ‘begang’ is ‘course, extent’. The semicolon closes what the visitors are, and the next unit gives their leader.

sentences.t:
þone yldestan ōretmecgas
Bēowulf nemnað.
sentences.l: the eldest, the warriors Beowulf name.
sentences.i: Their eldest the warriors call Beowulf.
sentences.n: The word order is object first: ‘þone yldestan’ is the accusative ‘the eldest’, ‘ōretmecgas’ the subject (‘battle-men’, as at 332: the Geat warriors themselves, so ‘their eldest’ is the eldest of their own number), and ‘nemnað’ the plural of ‘nemnan’, ‘name, call’, with the name ‘Bēowulf’ as the second object. ‘yldestan’ is the superlative of ‘eald’, used in Fitt IV of the leader of the band (‘se yldesta’), so it may mean either oldest or foremost. Wulfgār repeats the name Beowulf gave at 343.

sentences.l: They are petitioners, that they, my lord, with you may exchange with words;
sentences.i: They are suppliants, asking that they may exchange words with you, my lord;
sentences.n: ‘Hȳ’ is a spelling of ‘hīe’, ‘they’, as in Fitt IV, and ‘bēnan’ is the plural of ‘bēna’, ‘petitioner’ (the singular is at 350). ‘þæt hīe … mōton wordum wrixlan’ is ‘that they may exchange words’, with ‘mōton’ the present plural of ‘mōtan’, ‘may, be allowed’, and ‘wrixlan’ (‘to exchange’) taking the dative ‘wordum’, ‘with words’. ‘wið þē’ is ‘with you’, and ‘þēoden mīn’ is a vocative, ‘my lord’, set inside the clause. The semicolon ends the request.

sentences.t:
nō ðū him wearne getēoh
ðīnra gegncwida, glædman Hrōðgār!
sentences.l: not you to them refusal grant of your replies, glad-man Hrothgar!
sentences.i: Do not deny them your reply, gracious Hrothgar!
sentences.n: ‘nō ðū … getēoh’ is a negative command: ‘getēoh’ is the imperative of ‘getēon’, ‘to grant, give’, so ‘do not grant’, and ‘him’ is ‘to them’. ‘wearne’ is ‘refusal’, and ‘wearne getēon’ means ‘to grant a refusal’, that is, ‘to refuse’; this sense is read from the parts. ‘ðīnra gegncwida’ is a genitive plural, ‘of your replies’, depending on ‘wearne’. ‘glædman’ is a vocative describing Hrothgar. The apparatus gives three readings: ‘glædman’ as one word (Klaeber), ‘glæd man’ as two (some earlier editors, abbreviated in the apparatus) and ‘glædmōd’, ‘glad-minded’ (two others). ‘Gracious’ is a guess within that range. The exclamation mark ends the request.

sentences.t:
Hȳ on wīggetāwum wyrðe þinceað
eorla geæhtlan;
sentences.l: They in war-gear worthy seem of earls' esteem;
sentences.i: In their war-gear they seem worthy of the regard of nobles;
sentences.n: ‘Hȳ … wyrðe þinceað’ is ‘they seem worthy’, with ‘þinceað’ the plural of ‘þyncan’, ‘seem’. ‘wyrðe’ takes a genitive, here ‘geæhtlan’ with ‘eorla’: ‘worthy of the esteem of earls’. ‘geæhtlan’ is rare and its sense is a guess, ‘esteem, regard’, from the notion of reckoning something's value. ‘wīggetāwum’ is a dative plural, ‘war-gear’ (‘wīg’, ‘war’; ‘getāwa’, ‘equipment’). The apparatus records that a string of editors, Sedgefield among them, read ‘wīggeatwum’ (‘geatwe’, ‘equipment’), the same meaning from another stem, and sends the reader to ‘T.C. § 23’, a numbered section that this transcription does not include, so what it says is not known here; the apparatus cites the same section again at 395, where the same two forms are in question. The semicolon sets the next judgment beside this one.

sentences.t:
hūru se aldor dēah,
sē þǣm heaðorincum hider wīsade.’
sentences.l: indeed the chief is of worth, he who the battle-men hither guided.’
sentences.i: and truly the chief is a worthy man, he who guided these warriors here.’
sentences.n: ‘hūru’ is ‘indeed, truly’. ‘se aldor’ is the subject, ‘the chief’ (the word of ‘aldre’ at 346), and ‘dēah’ is the present singular of ‘dugan’, ‘be good, be worth something’, the verb behind ‘duguð’ at 359. ‘sē … wīsade’ is a relative clause, ‘he who guided’, with the past of ‘wīsian’ and the dative ‘þǣm heaðorincum’, ‘the battle-men’ (‘heaðo’, ‘battle’; ‘rinc’, ‘man’); ‘hider’ is ‘hither’. The leader is Beowulf, the ‘yldestan’ of 363. The closing mark ends Wulfgār's speech, and with it the part.
